diagnostic_tracker.title: Pattern Parade — Day 1 Diagnostic Checklist (Grade 1)
diagnostic_tracker.when_used: During Lesson 1, while children are in the partner-build phase of the Action segment.
diagnostic_tracker.usage_notes: Walk between pairs during the partner-build activity. For each child, tick the columns where you see clear evidence; leave blank if not yet observed (rather than marking 'no'). The 'Justifies prediction' column is the new Grade 1 marker — it separates children who pattern-match from children who reason. The 'Creates 3-element pattern' column is the key signal for which children are already operating above grade and can be challenged in Lessons 2–5. Children with blanks across the first three columns may need a small-group re-loop on Lesson 1 before continuing to rule-naming in Lesson 2.
diagnostic_tracker.layout_description: One letter page, portrait orientation. Title at the top, expectation focus (C1.1) in a small box below. A date field and class label in the header row. The body is a table with one column for student names (left, ~1.4in wide), five narrow tick columns (~0.8in each) labelled with the column names, and a Notes column on the right (~1.6in wide). Approximately 24 blank student rows so the page accommodates a typical Ontario Grade 1 class.

formative_trackers.title: Pattern Parade — Lesson 2 Formative Tracker (Naming the Rule)
formative_trackers.when_used: During Lesson 2, while children are in the partner phase of Lasso the Core, Name the Rule.
formative_trackers.usage_notes: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Where is the core?' and 'What is the rule?' to elicit the first two columns. To check column 3 (extends), point past the strip and ask 'and cell 8?'. Column 4 (justifies with rule language) is the deepest signal — children who say 'because the rule is ABB' have internalized the rule as a tool, not just a label. Children who can identify and label but cannot use the rule to extend are often almost-there — give them one more opportunity to articulate before moving on.

formative_trackers.title: Pattern Parade — Lesson 3 Formative Tracker (Translating the Rule)
formative_trackers.when_used: During Lesson 3, while pairs are translating their assigned rule into sound and body versions in the Action phase.
columns: Names what stayed the same (the rule)
formative_trackers.usage_notes: Translation columns should reflect whether the structural rule is preserved, not whether the surface elements look polished. A child who claps clap-stomp-stomp matching their ABB animal pattern has succeeded — even if the claps are loud or quiet. The 'Names what stayed the same' column captures abstraction (Level 3 of C1.2). The 'Uses rule label' column captures the Grade 1 leap of using formal letter notation when explaining — a child who only describes things ('the bears and the foxes') has not yet reached Level 3.
formative_trackers.layout_description: Identical layout to the diagnostic tracker but with the Lesson 3 column names. Title and expectation box updated to reflect C1.2 focus.

formative_trackers.title: Pattern Parade — Lesson 4 Formative Tracker (Detective Parade)
formative_trackers.when_used: During Lesson 4, while pairs are working through the Detectives at Work — Fix and Extend phase.
formative_trackers.usage_notes: The columns are deliberately separated by gap position because difficulty differs: middle and end are easier than start; forward is easier than backward. Justifying with rule language (e.g., 'because the rule is ABB') is the C1.3 capstone — children who can do this independently have reached Level 3. A child solid on middle/end and forward but blank on start/backward is on track for the typical Grade 1 trajectory — those skills sometimes don't fully consolidate until late G1 or Grade 2. Use this tracker to identify children who already extend backward AND justify independently (ready for the summative on confidence) versus children who will need conferences in Lesson 5.
formative_trackers.layout_description: Identical layout to the diagnostic tracker but with the Lesson 4 column names (one extra column compared to L2/L3 because Detective Parade has multiple sub-skills). Title and expectation box updated.

summative_rubric.title: Pattern Parade — Grade 1 Summative Rubric
summative_rubric.purpose: Used during and after Lesson 5 (Lead the Number Parade) to score each child against all four Grade 1 expectations on a 4-level scale. Aligned with Ontario Grade 1 conventions: descriptive, observational, and growth-oriented, with Level 3 as the grade-level expectation.

rows.expectation_text: identify and describe the regularities in a variety of patterns, including patterns found in real-life contexts

levels.descriptor: With significant adult prompting, identifies what comes next in a 2-element repeating pattern only some of the time. Does not yet describe the repeating part or create a pattern independently.

Predicts the next element in a 2- or 3-element repeating pattern most of the time. Describes the repeating part with prompting. Creates a repeating pattern with two elements when given a partner and a starter.

Confidently identifies, describes, and predicts in repeating patterns of 2 or 3 elements (animal, sound, shape, or letter). Independently creates a repeating pattern with two or three elements and explains the repeating part.

Spontaneously identifies repeating patterns in the classroom environment and across representations (numbers, letters, shapes, objects). Creates patterns with 3- or 4-element cores and predicts elements far beyond what is shown using the rule.

rows.expectation_text: create and translate patterns using movements, sounds, objects, shapes, letters, and numbers

levels.descriptor: Treats different representations of the same rule as different patterns. Surface-feature thinking dominates ('they are not the same because one has bears and one has claps').

With teacher modelling, can produce one second representation of a given rule, but the structure often drifts (e.g., ABB animal turns into AABB sound). Names what changed but not what stayed the same.

Independently translates a given rule (AB, ABB, AAB, or ABC) into 2 different representations from objects, sounds, movements, or pictures. Articulates that the rule stayed the same and only the things changed.

Translates one rule into 3 or more representations including invented ones (e.g., shapes, letters, numbers). Uses the rule label spontaneously when explaining and offers the same translation back to a new rule on the spot.

rows.expectation_text: determine pattern rules and use them to extend patterns, make and justify predictions, and identify missing elements in patterns

levels.descriptor: Cannot consistently isolate the core or name a rule. Fills missing cells with random animals. Cannot justify a prediction beyond a guess ('I just thought it').

Identifies the core in simple AB patterns and labels it AB with prompting. Fills missing elements at the end of a pattern. Justifies with surface description ('because the bear comes back') rather than rule language.

Independently identifies the core in AB, ABB, AAB, and ABC patterns and names the rule. Fills missing elements anywhere in the pattern (including the start, with some prompting). Justifies predictions using rule language ('because the rule is ABB').

Names rules invented by classmates immediately. Extends patterns in both directions independently, including reasoning backward from a single given cell. Justifies predictions far beyond the visible pattern (e.g., 'cell 20 would be Bea because the rule is ABB and 20 divided by 3 lands on the A').

rows.expectation_text: create and describe patterns to illustrate relationships among whole numbers up to 50

levels.descriptor: Does not yet translate an animal parade into a number parade. May write random or counting numbers (1, 2, 3) instead of repeating numbers. Does not connect rule labels to numbers.
With teacher prompting, builds a 2-element repeating number parade using small numbers (1–10). Describes the rule using letter labels but not the relationship between the numbers.

Independently builds a repeating number parade up to 50 using two or three numbers and a chosen rule. Explains how the numbers in the parade follow the rule (e.g., 'A is 10 and B is 25 and the rule AB makes them take turns').
Builds repeating number parades using larger numbers within 50 and ABC or invented rules. Predicts numbers in cells far beyond what is shown using the rule and the relationship between A, B, and C.

summative_rubric.usage_notes: Score during the Lesson 5 Plan-Build-Translate-Lead phases (most evidence is visible from the worksheet) and confirm during the Lead phase (partner observation). Level 3 is the grade-level expectation; aim for most children to land at L2 or L3 by end-of-unit. L1 is a signal for additional support; L4 is a signal for enrichment in Grade 2. Communicate scores to families using descriptive language alongside the level (e.g., 'Achieving Level 3 — independently builds and explains repeating patterns with a chosen rule, including using whole numbers up to 50') rather than letter grades.
summative_rubric.layout_description: One letter page, landscape orientation, with a 4×4 grid table (4 expectation rows × 4 level columns) plus a left-most column for the expectation code and text. Each cell contains the level descriptor in K/G1-readable type. Title at the top of the page; usage notes printed below the table. Light-grey shading on the Level 3 column to signal that Level 3 is the goal level. Total table approximately 10in wide × 6.5in tall.

summative_task_script.title: Lead the Number Parade — Summative Administration Guide (Grade 1)
summative_task_script.purpose: Ties the Lesson 5 worksheet, the lesson plan's four phases (Plan-Build-Translate-Lead), and the rubric together. Tells the teacher exactly what evidence to look for during each phase and which expectation each phase's evidence maps to.
administration_steps: Before the lesson: photocopy one summative worksheet ('Lead the Number Parade') per child. Print one rubric per child or maintain a single class rubric on a clipboard with student-name rows pre-filled. Have the Junior Pattern Conductor certificates printed and ready for the closing ceremony (do not show them to children before they have earned them). Confirm the hundred chart 0–50 is visible on the math wall.

Phase 1 (Plan, 5 min): Children write their rule (AB/ABB/AAB/ABC) in My Rule and draw their core in My Core. This produces visible evidence for C1.3 (rule identification). Walk the room and check that each child has a rule AND a matching core; nudge children whose rule and core do not match.

Phase 2 (Build animal parade, 8 min): Children fill the 8-cell animal parade and loop the first core. This produces visible evidence for C1.1 (creates a pattern using the rule) and confirms C1.3. Begin one-on-one rubric conferences during this phase — ask each child to read their parade aloud and answer 'what would cell 9 be? How do you know?'.

Phase 3 (Translate to numbers, 8 min): Children fill the My Number Key (A = ___, B = ___, optional C = ___) with numbers 1–50 and complete the 8-cell number parade using the same rule. This produces evidence for C1.4 (number parade up to 50) AND C1.2 (translating to a different representation). Continue rubric conferences. By end of Phase 3 you should have scored most children on at least 3 of 4 expectations.

Phase 4 (Lead, 7 min): Children pair up on the carpet and lead each other through their parade — animals first, then numbers. Listen for partners articulating the rule, predicting what comes next in both parades, and explaining the relationship between the animals and the numbers. Use this phase to confirm uncertain rubric scores and upgrade scores where Level 4 thinking shows up.

After the lesson: review the rubric with the worksheet artifact in front of you. For any child below Level 3 on any expectation, note what evidence (or absence) drove that decision. Use this for the report-card narrative. Also review the bottom-of-worksheet justify sentence — a child who wrote (or had scribed) a rule-referenced explanation has Level 3 evidence on C1.3 even if their oral conference was tentative.
summative_task_script.scoring_guidance: Use the worksheet as primary evidence and the partner-lead conversation as confirming evidence. For each expectation, ask: 'What level of independence and confidence did this child show?' Level 3 is the grade-level goal — aim for most children to land at L2 or L3 by end-of-unit. Children who are L4 on every expectation are ready for Grade 2 pattern work (growing and shrinking patterns); document this for the receiving teacher. Children who are L1 on multiple expectations need targeted small-group work in the next math block, especially around the new Grade 1 vocabulary (rule, justify) and the number-parade translation.

evidence_per_expectation.C1.1: Look at Part 2 of the worksheet (animal parade). Did the child create a valid 8-cell repeating pattern using their chosen rule? Combined with their My Core box. A child who fills Part 2 with a coherent repetition of their rule is at Level 3 on C1.1. A child who also uses 3-element cores (ABB, AAB, ABC) without prompting is at Level 4.
evidence_per_expectation.C1.2: Look at Part 3 (number parade). Does the number parade use the SAME structural rule as the animal parade in Part 2? A child who fills Part 3 with numbers that follow the same rule (e.g., AAB animal becomes AAB number) is at Level 3 on C1.2 — they have translated. A child who drifts in structure (animal AAB becomes number ABB) is at Level 2.
evidence_per_expectation.C1.3: Look at Part 1 (My Rule and My Core boxes) AND the bottom-of-page justify sentence. Did the child write a rule label that matches their core? Did they justify with rule language ('because the rule is ___')? Combined with the partner-lead conversation in Phase 4 ('how do you know cell 9 is ___?'). A child who writes both correctly AND justifies aloud with rule language is at Level 3.
evidence_per_expectation.C1.4: Look at the My Number Key in Part 3. Did the child pick numbers between 1 and 50 (not just 1–10)? Did the number parade preserve the rule? A child who picks any two valid numbers between 1 and 50 and builds the parade correctly is at Level 3. A child who only used very small numbers (1, 2) is at Level 2 (the relationship is correct but the up-to-50 range is unproven). A child who used larger numbers AND can explain the relationship between A and B as numbers (e.g., 'A is 10 and B is 25, B is bigger') is at Level 4.

certificate.title: Junior Pattern Conductor Certificate
certificate.recipient_field_label: This certificate is proudly presented to:
certificate.achievement_text: For successfully completing the 5-Day Pattern Parade unit, naming pattern rules, translating across representations, and leading a number parade up to 50.
skills_demonstrated: Spotting and creating repeating patterns and predicting what comes next
Naming pattern rules using letters (AB, ABB, AAB, ABC)
Showing one rule in many different ways — animals, sounds, bodies, and numbers
Finding missing elements anywhere in a parade and justifying predictions using the rule
Building a repeating number parade with whole numbers up to 50
certificate.layout_description: One letter page, portrait orientation. Decorative ornamental border around the entire page (~0.5in margin). Title 'Junior Pattern Conductor Certificate' at the top in large ornate font (~1in tall). Below: the recipient label and a wide blank line for the child's name. Below: the achievement text. Below: a bullet list of the five skills demonstrated. Toward the bottom: two side-by-side signature lines labelled 'Teacher Signature' and 'Date'. At the bottom-centre, a small Coco the Conductor illustration holding his baton in a celebratory pose. Designed to feel celebratory and ceremonial — not utilitarian.
